segments: The desktop, toolkit, compositor, and input method all affect the windows you ultimately see. When troubleshooting, first identify the path messages take, then determine which component draws a particular visual element. Avoid reducing every problem to “try a different theme.”
Qt, GTK, and display protocols operate at different layers

Qt and GTK are application toolkits that provide widgets, events, and application interfaces. Wayland and X11 are window-system protocols and mechanisms; the same toolkit can use different display backends. A Qt application is not necessarily an X11 application, and a GTK application is not necessarily part of a particular desktop environment.

XWayland provides compatibility for X11 applications in a Wayland session. A process running in a Wayland session does not prove that its window is using a native Wayland backend. Check the window’s actual backend before explaining why an environment variable does or does not take effect.
Input-method communication paths and candidate windows

The input engine converts input into candidates; the frontend connects input protocols from applications, toolkits, or compositors to Fcitx5; the user interface then displays candidates and status. Engines such as Rime and Pinyin operate at a different layer from candidate-window themes.

Applications can communicate with Fcitx5 through GTK / Qt input-method modules, or through Wayland text-input with the compositor connecting them to the input method. The original note’s claim that “native Wayland input always has the application draw the candidate window itself” was too absolute: the protocol path and the candidate-panel implementation must be checked separately. Support in the environment affects Classic UI, panel integration, and fallback paths; Qt6, GTK4, or a terminal’s name alone cannot establish whether a theme will definitely work or definitely fail.
Match environment variables to the specific application

XMODIFIERS primarily concerns X11 / XWayland; GTK_IM_MODULE and QT_IM_MODULE affect the choices made by their respective toolkits. Setting more variables does not necessarily improve compatibility. Forcing an input-method module may bypass the Wayland text-input path you intended to use, or may be necessary for a specific application that does not support that path.

KDE Plasma, GNOME, and wlroots-based compositors differ in their support for input-method protocols. The Qt version, whether an application bundles input-method modules, and whether XWayland is enabled also affect the outcome. Choose settings using the upstream Fcitx5 application/compositor matrix; apply per-application overrides for special cases rather than setting the whole group of variables globally without checking.

When troubleshooting, record the application version, display backend, toolkit version, compositor, relevant environment variables, and Fcitx5 logs. Then compare a working application with a malfunctioning one in the same environment to narrow down the differences.
Compositors, desktop shells, and status bars

Hyprland and Niri primarily handle window management, input, output layout, and compositing. A desktop shell provides interfaces such as panels, launchers, notifications, and a control center. Quickshell is a framework for implementing these interfaces; it should not be treated as the same product as a particular shell.

Noctalia, DMS, Waybar, and full desktop environments have different responsibilities and integration approaches. Waybar is primarily a status bar; Quickshell lets developers define interfaces and logic; KDE Plasma / GNOME provide more complete desktop integration. These are not successive upgrade tiers, and no particular combination is inherently guaranteed to be faster.
Application rendering paths and performance assessment

Frameworks such as Qt / GTK, Electron, and Flutter make different choices about widgets, rendering, and system integration. Applications still ultimately present their output through the window system. This cannot be represented as a single path in which an application passes through the desktop shell before reaching the GPU; the shell itself is also a client or desktop component involved in compositing.

Assess performance through processes, frame times, resource use, and actual interaction. Whether a static interface saves memory cannot be deduced from labels such as “native” or “GPU UI” alone; blur, animations, image decoding, and refresh rates can all change the load.
Locate appearance and input problems layer by layer
Confirm the application’s actual display backend and version rather than relying only on the session name.
Check whether the input-method engine produces candidates and whether the application receives preedit and committed text.
Identify the UI implementation that displays the candidate panel, then check its theme, fonts, and scaling.
Check compositor protocols and toolkit input-method modules, then address application-specific fallbacks.
Change only one layer at a time, reproduce the issue with the same input, and retain reversible configurations and logs.

For further study, explore Wayland text-input, toolkit input contexts, compositor input-method support, the Rime engine, and QML interfaces separately. Distinguish the interfaces first, then decide which configuration to change.
